case_study_insert.main_stem: Bluecrest Airport Shuttle (BAS) is a private limited company in the passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Priya Nandakumar, the business runs a fleet of coaches and minibuses carrying passengers between Westmoor International Airport and the surrounding towns, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. BAS plans to invest $720,000 in six electric shuttle buses and charging infrastructure, financed by a $450,000 seven-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. BAS faces rising driver absenteeism, which reached 8% last quarter, and two new competitors have started undercutting its airport fares.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The shuttle fleet completed 25,400 passenger journeys last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1% (unplanned breakdowns), down from 3.4% a year ago. On-time departures improved to 91.5%. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 17 per month. Market research of 500 airport passengers found 58% would pay up to $0.30 more for guaranteed-seat bookings, and 46% prefer electric vehicles. A skills audit shows 3 of 38 drivers still need electric-vehicle certification (off-the-job training at the local college costs $750 per driver; on-the-job training is unavailable in-house).

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Bluecrest Airport Shuttle for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing repayments on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $11.93 to $12.71 per hour from April 2026, raising staff costs. (3) Grid electricity prices for charging depots have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and consumer spending on airport transfers grew 4.2%, with transport and leisure inflation running at 7.6%.

questions.question_text: BAS plans to finance the expansion with a $450,000 seven-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for BAS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of relying solely on the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs BAS nothing in interest or repayments, which protects cash flow while it already services the $450,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $270,000 a year. Every dollar not paid out as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in grid electricity costs, helping BAS hold the $9.00 selling price against two new competitors undercutting its airport fares and defending its $5.40 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so if passenger numbers at Westmoor International Airport dip, BAS would not be forced to sell coaches to meet loan repayments. Funding $270,000 this way also preserves the democratic, flat structure that Priya Nandakumar created: no external lender can impose conditions on how the six electric shuttle buses are routed, priced or timetabled, and ownership remains entirely with existing shareholders, avoiding dilution or lender interference as the business invests $720,000 in its future.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bluecrest Airport Shuttle and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: BAS is launching its electric airport shuttle service. Consider airport terminal advertising boards, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should BAS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Airport terminal advertising boards: Advertising inside Westmoor International Airport reaches arriving and departing passengers at the exact point of need, building instant awareness of the new electric shuttle. High footfall and captive dwell times give strong visibility, and the format suits a service whose entire market is airport passengers. However, airport media contracts are expensive for a 38-employee business funding a $720,000 expansion, and they reach only passengers already at the airport, not residents or workers who could use the service for commuting or hotel transfers.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is far cheaper than airport media, supports time-sensitive launch messages such as 'new electric shuttle now running', and reaches the towns BAS serves, matching its fixed route network. Its limitation is that many listeners will never use an airport shuttle, so wastage is high, and coverage stops at the regional boundary, capping the volume of passengers BAS can attract for its 100,000 units a year.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with local travel, family and sustainability influencers targets the 58% of 500 surveyed passengers willing to pay up to $0.30 more for guaranteed-seat bookings and the 46% who prefer electric vehicles, telling the electric story directly to engaged audiences with measurable likes, clicks and bookings at low cost per reached customer. Influencer trust builds more slowly than airport boards and depends on influencer fit, but spend can be scaled, paused or redirected quickly.

Recommendation: BAS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches precisely the passengers BAS's research shows will pay a premium, costs far less than airport terminal contracts, scales beyond the local radio audience, and reinforces the eco-friendly positioning that city commuters increasingly expect. Airport terminal advertising is rejected as too costly and captive-market only; local radio is rejected as too narrow for routes serving hotels, towns and the airport itself; influencer campaigns should be supported with modest stands at the terminal during peak summer months.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BAS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BAS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why airport terminal advertising and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: BAS's driver absenteeism reached 8% last quarter. Explain two benefits for BAS of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its driving team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives BAS's 38 employees a genuine voice in shift patterns, route timings and on-board service standards, which supports their social and esteem needs and lifts job satisfaction. Drivers who help design rotas that fit airport arrival peaks are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the 8% absenteeism rate and reducing the strain on the flat structure and on Priya Nandakumar, who currently fields most operational decisions personally.

Point 2: Involving drivers in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who meet passengers every day, improving punctuality beyond the current 91.5% on-time figure and cutting the 2.1% defect rate of unplanned breakdowns by flagging maintenance issues earlier. Higher involvement increases commitment and lowers staff turnover, saving the $750 per driver certification cost and protecting 100,000 units a year of output while the six electric buses bed in and fixed costs of $270,000 are covered. Reliable, engaged crews also feed directly into the guaranteed-seat promise, which the 58% who will pay up to $0.30 more are willing to book precisely because BAS turns up on time.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BAS's absenteeism, punctuality and output.

questions.question_text: BAS must upskill the 3 drivers who lack electric-vehicle certification so they can operate the new fleet. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should BAS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside an experienced EV driver passes on BAS's own routines — charging etiquette, route times, passenger care and fault reporting — at zero course fees, and the 3 drivers keep earning while they learn, protecting the 25,400 passenger journeys completed last quarter and the 91.5% on-time rate. Drawbacks are that BAS has no in-house EV specialist, so coaching could transmit bad habits or unsafe charging practice, and no recognised certificate results, which may weaken insurance or airport authority compliance for the new $720,000 bus fleet.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per driver costs only $2,250 in total, gives structured, up-to-date high-voltage safety and battery knowledge, and awards a recognised certificate for all 3 drivers. Taking drivers off the road reduces short-term capacity during peak airport season, and generic content may not match BAS's exact bus models, so some route-specific coaching on return would still be needed.

Decision: BAS should choose off-the-job training at the local college, topped up with short on-the-job route coaching. High-voltage EV operation carries safety and compliance stakes that make a proper certificate essential, and $2,250 is trivial against a $720,000 investment; the off-the-job route also avoids passing on unsafe habits during a period when absenteeism is already 8%. On-the-job-only training is rejected because BAS lacks an in-house EV expert and uncertificated drivers would jeopardise the electric fleet launch and airport compliance, while full off-the-job delivery without any route coaching would leave drivers unfamiliar with BAS's own schedules, so a combined approach is safest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BAS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of BAS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of BAS with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety, compliance and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BAS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($9.00 − $3.60) = $270,000 ÷ $5.40 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.00 − $3.60 = $5.40. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BAS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BAS can compare its 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units to confirm the service is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 50,000 units, informing decisions on whether to extend electric routes beyond the airport.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.40 lets BAS model fare promotions, for example a 10% discount to $8.10 would cut contribution to $4.50, letting managers test whether the extra ticket volume would still cover fixed costs of $270,000 before running a price campaign.
3. Knowing contribution per unit helps managers check the expansion is bankable: the new electric fleet must generate enough journeys to service the $450,000 bank loan alongside $270,000 fixed costs, so sales targets can be tied directly to repayment schedules.
4. Unit cost data ($270,000 ÷ 100,000 units + $3.60 = $6.30 a unit) lets managers benchmark each quarter, spot waste driving the 2.1% breakdown defect rate and the 8% absenteeism, and renegotiate the $3.60 variable cost with fuel and parts suppliers as electricity prices rise 9.8%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.40 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 50,000 units vs 100,000-unit output; discount modelling against $270,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $720,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $6.30 to tackle waste and absenteeism.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BAS's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BAS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 42.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 figures ($'000): gross profit $336,000 ÷ revenue $800,000 × 100 = 42.0%; 2025: gross profit $387,000 ÷ revenue $900,000 × 100 = 43.0%. Operating profit against revenue: 2024: $96,000 ÷ $800,000 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025: $135,000 ÷ $900,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed: 2024: $96,000 ÷ $600,000 × 100 = 16.0%; 2025: $135,000 ÷ $675,000 × 100 = 20.0%. Cost of sales rose from $464,000 to $513,000 as volumes grew, but fell as a share of revenue from 58.0% to 57.0%, and capital employed rose from $600,000 to $675,000 as the electric fleet investment entered the accounts.

Evaluation: Profitability has clearly strengthened across every measure. Revenue grew 12.5% from $800,000 to $900,000, consistent with BAS moving toward 100,000 units a year. Gross profit improved from 42.0% to 43.0%, suggesting BAS controlled variable costs of $3.60 a unit well despite the 9.8% rise in grid electricity prices. Operating profit improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, meaning overheads were controlled even while interest payable rose from $18,000 to $26,000 on the larger loan. Operating profit against capital employed jumped from 16.0% to 20.0%, so the expansion is generating an improving return on the money tied up in the business — essential while BAS funds a $720,000 fleet renewal. Weaknesses remain: interest payable is rising, margins are still moderate for a transport operator, and the figures depend on sustaining Westmoor passenger volumes against two undercutting competitors.

Conclusion: BAS's financial performance has improved. Gross profit (42.0% to 43.0%), operating profit against revenue (12.0% to 15.0%) and operating profit against capital employed (16.0% to 20.0%) all moved in the right direction with revenue growth to back them. The business should nevertheless watch interest costs and competitor pricing, and keep driving the 9.8% electricity-cost pressure out of its operations to lock in these gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether BAS's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BAS of introducing electric shuttle buses into its fleet.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Electric shuttle buses match the preferences of the 46% of 500 surveyed passengers who prefer electric vehicles and the 58% willing to pay up to $0.30 more for guaranteed-seat bookings, letting BAS charge a premium that protects its $5.40 contribution per unit. Zero tailpipe emissions also strengthen BAS's brand image with environmentally minded airport passengers and councils setting airport clean-air targets, supporting contract renewals at Westmoor International Airport and justifying the $720,000 investment.

Disadvantage: Electric buses cost more to buy than diesel equivalents and require charging infrastructure, adding to the $450,000 bank loan burden before revenue arrives. Range and charging downtime could also trim daily route capacity, while the 9.8% rise in grid electricity prices inflates the $3.60 variable cost per unit, squeezing margins unless the $0.30 premium is accepted across the fleet and charging is scheduled off-peak. Any reliability teething problems could push the 2.1% defect rate back toward 3.4% before the new buses bed in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BAS's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase to $12.71 and the 9.8% rise in grid electricity costs will affect BAS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If BAS's $450,000 seven-year loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $3,375 a year in interest, nudging interest payable above the current $26,000 (per Appendix 2) and slightly increasing the strain on fixed costs of $270,000 a year. Higher rates also make consumers and businesses more cautious on discretionary travel spending and raise the cost of any future borrowing for further fleet growth. The direct cash hit is real but modest, and BAS can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $12.71 per hour): With a workforce of 38, mainly drivers and depot staff, BAS's wage bill rises by roughly 6.5%. If average hourly pay is around $12.71, annual wages per full-time employee are roughly $26,500, so the rise adds about $1,700 per worker or around $65,000 across the workforce — a much larger cash impact than the interest rise, and one BAS must offset through productivity (100,000 units ÷ 38 staff ≈ 2,632 units per worker), the democratic leadership approach and absenteeism reduction.

Grid electricity cost rise (9.8%): For the new electric fleet, electricity is effectively the fuel line inside BAS's $3.60 variable cost per unit. A 9.8% rise adds roughly $0.20–$0.35 per unit; across 100,000 units a year that is $20,000–$35,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $5.40 toward $5.05–$5.20 and trimming profit, although off-peak charging contracts and the $0.30 guaranteed-seat premium can recover much of this. Electricity also underpins the whole eco-positioning of the expansion.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in grid electricity costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes BAS's operating model directly and repeatedly, eroding the $5.40 contribution on every one of its 100,000 annual units and undermining the economics of the $720,000 electric expansion it is rolling out now. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious pressure, adding roughly $65,000 a year, while the interest rate rise is the smallest in cash terms and can be managed by fixing the loan; all three demand disciplined cost control, off-peak charging and premium pricing such as the $0.30 guaranteed-seat fee.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BAS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BAS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BAS with a well-justified judgment that the electricity cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
